title: KV cache shadow-compact and priority backpressure playbook
content:
Context:
This is a working playbook that explores two complementary ideas to reduce long-tail latency and fragmentation in the KV cache: (1) a lightweight "shadow compact" path that opportunistically compacts cold/fragmented segments without blocking hot request paths, and (2) a per-request priority backpressure system that gates admission and scheduling when the cache is approaching fragmentation or memory-pressure thresholds.

Goals:
- Reduce memory fragmentation and long-term occupancy growth without introducing high-p99 stalls.
- Prefer short, incremental compaction over heavy stop-the-world rewrites.
- Protect latency SLOs by throttling lower-priority traffic early rather than forcing synchronous eviction on hot lanes.
- Provide observability and controls to tune compaction aggressiveness and backpressure policies.

Constraints and assumptions:
- Serving runtime runs multiple cache shards per-GPU and must avoid cross-shard global pauses.
- Most workload is read-heavy (prefix reuse) with occasional model-variant churn causing many short-lived entries.
- We have existing request-priority propagation (api-tier assigns priority tokens) that we can reuse.
- Compaction should be preemptible and able to yield to tail requests.

Key concepts introduced here:
1) Shadow compact: a background, read-friendly compaction worker that creates compacted copies of fragmented segments and swaps pointers atomically when ready.
2) Granular eviction lanes: segregate entries into hot, warm, cold lanes; eviction/backpressure decisions happen per-lane and per-shard.
3) Priority backpressure token-buckets: requests carry a priority label; low-priority requests may be delayed or rejected under pressure.
4) Compactness score: sampled metadata sketch per-segment that estimates fragmentation, live density, and rewrite benefit.

Design - Shadow compact
- Segment layout:
  - Cache is organized into fixed-size segments (e.g., 256KB) grouped into slabs by segment-size-classes.
  - Each segment has a small header with: generation id, compactness score, last-access epoch, and a compact-write-offset.
- Shadow compact worker behavior:
  - Operates as N soft workers per-shard (configurable) running at low priority; they pick candidate segments with compactness score < threshold AND last-access > cold-window.
  - Worker allocates a new segment (from free pool) and copies only live entries (based on per-entry tombstone/TTL) into it. Copy is rate-limited by a throughput budget and can be paused if pipeline sees p99 latency spikes.
  - After building the new segment, worker attempts an atomic swap of the segment pointer under a narrow CAS/lock. Swap succeeds only if the original segment's generation id hasn't changed. On CAS failure, worker aborts and frees the new segment (or retries a bounded number of times).
  - The old segment is enqueued for safe reclamation once all in-flight references are drained (RCU or epoch-based reclamation).
- Partial compaction:
  - If a segment has a small hot prefix and large cold tail, worker may create two resulting segments: hot-prefix kept in-place, cold-tail compacted to new segment and linked as separate. This reduces write amplification and avoids touching hot entries.

Design - Priority backpressure
- Priority model:
  - Requests arrive with priority {P0: system-critical, P1: interactive, P2: batch} propagated from API layer. Default is P1.
- Token-bucket gating per-lane:
  - Each shard exposes token buckets per-priority and per-lane (hot/warm/cold). Under normal conditions buckets are full. On memory pressure or high fragmentation ratio, we drain tokens from low priorities first.
  - When a request needs to insert a new entry, it must acquire an admission token for the target lane. If no token available, two options depending on policy: queue (bounded wait) or reject with 503+retry-after for batch.
- Cost accounting:
  - Each admission consumes tokens proportional to estimated entry size and expected lifetime (sampled from histograms). This discourages large ephemeral inserts from starving the system.

Compactness scoring and sampling
- We maintain a compactness sketch per-segment: sampled counters for live bytes, dead bytes, and entry count. Update on inserts/evicts asynchronously to avoid hot path cost.
- Compactness score = dead_bytes / total_bytes * log(entry_count + 1) — tuned to prefer compacting high-dead-ratio dense segments.
- Additionally, track an eviction-benefit estimate: expected reclaimable bytes per-second if compacted, using access-rate decay so we don't compact segments that will be re-populated quickly.

Observability and metrics
- Per-shard metrics to expose:
  - segment_count, avg_compactness_score, shadow_compactions_started/succeeded/failed, compaction_throughput_bytes/s, compaction_write_amp ratio, lane_admits_per_priority, lane_rejects_per_priority, p99_request_latency_by_priority.
- Alerts:
  - sustained avg_compactness_score < X for 5m => increase compaction budget or extend cold-window.
  - lane_rejects_per_priority[P1] > threshold => investigate compaction failures or raise memory limit.

Safety and preemption
- Shadow workers must be preemptible: they check a global p99-latency signal and yield if threshold crossed. They also obey per-shard compaction rate limits (bytes/sec) and an overall cluster budget.
- Atomic swap path is the only place that may introduce a short critical section; keep CAS/lock scope minimal and avoid copying during the lock.

Rollout plan
1. Canary stage: Enable shadow-compact in read-only mode (workers build compacts but do not swap). Emit detailed metrics and sample diffs to validate expected reclaim amounts.
2. Controlled swap: Enable swap only for cold segments (last-access > 1h) and for shards under low load. Measure latency impact and swap success rate.
3. Priority backpressure: Start with P2 gating only (batch), then gradually enable bounded queues for P1 under tight conditions.
4. Progressive tuning: Adjust thresholds (compactness_score, cold-window), worker counts, and token-bucket rates based on observed metrics.

Simulation and validation tests
- Create workload generator with mix: 85% reads, 10% small writes, 5% large writes; inject model-rollout churn bursts that create many short-lived entries.
- Simulate varying shard counts and per-GPU memory pressures, measure p50/p90/p99 latency, write amplification, reclaimed bytes, and compaction CPU usage.
- Run fault-injection where CAS swap fails repeatedly to validate retry/backoff and resource reclamation.

Open questions / discussion items:
- Optimal compactness formula: does including access-rate decay improve ranking enough to justify the extra metadata?
- Should we allow priority promotion (batch -> interactive) if retries fail often? Risk of priority inversion.
- How aggressive should partial compaction be for segments with hot prefixes? Tradeoff between pointer complexity and reclaim.
- Integration with existing slab classes and NUMA arenas: ensure new allocation patterns don't cause cross-NUMA thrash.

Action items (next steps):
- [Aisha] build canary worker implementation (no-swap) and metric hooks (2w).
- [Ravi] implement compactness sketch and sampling APIs used by workers (1w).
- [Marta] add token-bucket admission prototype and integrate priority propagation from API (1.5w).
- Schedule simulation run and compare baseline eviction-only strategy vs shadow-compact + backpressure.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally lightweight and contains open design choices. Please comment directly with use-cases or workload properties you think will change thresholds (e.g., chat vs embed-heavy workloads).
- If you have seen similar designs in other systems (rocksdb/leveldb compaction heuristics, memcached eviction lanes), link the paper/notes here.
